title: Evaluation and Validation of Established Prognostic Markers in Patients with HNSCC-CUP (Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Unknown Primary)
summary:
General Overview:
This study investigates specific biological markers in rare head and neck tumors where the primary tumor cannot be identified despite extensive diagnostic workup (referred to as "HNSCC-CUP"). The aim is to determine whether markers such as p16, HPV, and the presence of extranodal extension can provide insights into the course of the disease and the response to therapy. Ultimately, this aims to improve diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and future treatment strategies.

In Detail:
Head and neck tumors are among the most common types of cancer worldwide, accounting for approximately 4.8% of all cancer-related deaths. Given the diverse manifestations of these tumors, individualized treatment is of particular importance.

A specific challenge is posed by so-called "Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Unknown Primary" (HNSCC-CUP). These cases involve metastases in the head and neck region where, despite extensive diagnostic investigations, the primary tumor cannot be located. Since the primary tumor remains unknown, both the selection of the optimal therapy and the assessment of the prognosis are rendered more difficult.

In recent years, various biological markers have been identified that can provide insights into the course of the disease and the response to therapy. These include the so-called p16 status, the HPV status, and the so-called extracapsular spread (ECS)—that is, the extension of tumor cells from a lymph node into the surrounding tissue.

The p16 status is determined via tissue staining and frequently serves as an indirect indicator of infection with human papillomaviruses (HPV). Both a positive p16 status and a positive HPV status are often associated with a better response to therapy. Conversely, the presence of ECS is frequently considered an unfavorable prognostic factor.

While the determination of p16 and ECS is already firmly established in routine clinical practice, the direct analysis of HPV DNA has only been routinely employed for a few years. Earlier assumptions posited that p16-positive tumors were, by definition, also HPV-positive. However, more recent studies demonstrate that p16 and HPV statuses do not always align. Such discrepancies can have implications for the course of the disease and the efficacy of therapy.

Consequently, for other (more common) head and neck tumors, the combined determination of p16 and HPV is now considered the standard of care. The prognostic significance of ECS also appears to be dependent on the HPV status.

In cases of HNSCC-CUP, p16, HPV, and ECS are likewise regarded as potential prognostic markers. However, there is currently limited scientific data regarding the concordance between p16 and HPV. Due to the rarity of this disease, only one small retrospective study—involving 32 patients and examining the discrepancies between p16 and HPV statuses—currently exists in Germany. Furthermore, data regarding the prognostic significance of the extent of ECS remain scarce. The aim of the present study is, therefore, to examine more closely the significance of p16 and HPV status, as well as ECS, in HNSCC-CUP, and to gain a better understanding of their influence on therapeutic response and disease course.
conditions: Malignant neoplasm, primary site unknown, so stated

interventions.name: Retrospective analysis of all patients for whom material from a squamous cell head and neck carcinoma with an unknown primary site is available since 2012.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck with unknown primary
Exclusion criteria:
Healthy or No Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck with Unknown Primary
